lines: Two plants buy the exact same model of machine tool from the exact same vendor.
One of them ends up with a long, flat list of raw addresses and a spreadsheet nobody has kept up to date.
The other plant's machine simply publishes a typed model of itself, with names, units and a hierarchy already built in.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal answers it.
One of those two plants gets this new machine fully onboarded in a matter of days, while the other takes months to get there.
What exactly did that typed model carry along with it that a raw, bare address never could have?
answer: It carried semantics the raw address simply never had.
The typed model attaches a name, a type, a unit, and a place in a hierarchy to every single value — exactly what the tag list left for some person to go figure out and maintain entirely by hand.

lines: In this model, every node is connected to other nodes through references, and each one of those references is its own specific, named type.
Starting from the machine itself and browsing down through its monitoring object and then its spindle object eventually reaches one particular variable.
That variable already carries its own data type and its own engineering unit, built right into the model itself.
A companion specification takes that exact same kind of path and standardizes it for an entire domain, once, for everyone.
Any machine tool built against that specification ends up exposing the very same object types as any other.
A client reading from it never has to build or maintain its own per-vendor map of tags just to make sense of what it's looking at.
A client can subscribe to a variable using what's called a monitored item, which only reports back once a value has moved past some stated threshold.
Measure that against simply polling the exact same signal over and over, reading every single sample along the way.
The monitored item ends up sending only a small fraction of the messages that plain polling would have sent for the very same signal.
In the client-server style of connecting, every single subscriber needs its own dedicated session with the server.
That means the total amount of notification traffic scales up directly with how many subscribers happen to be listening.
A publish-subscribe model decouples the publisher from whoever's subscribing, so its own message count doesn't scale that way at all.
The specification's own default security setting isn't actually set to no security at all.
Instead, that default is deliberately an invalid value, specifically so that no security can never end up chosen purely by accident.
Finding a real server out in a plant still configured with no security applied at all is therefore a genuine finding to raise, never something to treat as an acceptable default.
Pull the whole picture together: typed nodes joined by typed references, a companion specification that standardizes one single path across every vendor.
Add a deadband that meaningfully cuts down how much notification traffic gets sent, and a publish-subscribe model that decouples that cost from how many subscribers exist.
And underneath every bit of it, a security default that was deliberately built so that no security could never be chosen purely by accident.
One more case worth reasoning through before moving on.
Suppose all you're given are the fields that one single browsed variable node actually carries: its own name, its own type, its own unit, and its own place somewhere in a hierarchy.
Working only from those fields, could you actually rebuild this entire plant's whole equipment hierarchy from the model alone?
answer: The very references that connect a machine's objects all the way down to its individual variables already encode that whole hierarchy directly — that's the entire reason browsing a model like this replaces a spreadsheet in the first place.
